title: Tasers have more importance, inquest hears
subtitle: Day 1 of inquest into shooting death of man by police
article: A York police expert in officer use of force told an inquest into the death of a man shot by police in 2005 that he sees benefit in more front-line officers carrying Tasers.
Sgt. Norman Wray made the comment in response to a question posed by Kenneth English, father of Jeffrey George Black, during the first day of testimony today.
The inquest is at Aurora Town Hall.

"I see the advantage to it," Sgt. Wray said, providing his personal opinion. A decision to put conducted energy weapons into the hands of more York police officers would be made by Chief Armand La Barge, Sgt. Wray said earlier.
The law restricts which officers can carry a Taser. The vast majority of front-line officers cannot and in York, specifically, only tactical officers carry the weapon, the inquest heard.
However, Sgt. Wray also said he does not see the value of the province allowing for "warning shots" to be fired at suspects during arrest attempts.
Mr. Black, 21, died at Scarborough Hospital Grace Campus in 2005 after he was shot by a York officer during a confrontation near 30 Alden Rd., in south Markham.
A provincial review of the officer's actions found the shooting justified.
The three-woman, two-man jury hearing the inquest may make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths.

Forensic pathologist Dr. Jacqueline Parai, who conducted an autopsy on Mr. Black, also testified this morning he had small amounts of alcohol and THC in his blood at the time of his death. THC is the main psychoactive substance found in Cannabis.
Mr. Black bled to death after being shot twice.
Under the Coroners Act, an inquest is mandatory when a person dies while in custody.

On Oct. 18, 2005, at about 11:45 p.m., two York officers responded to an alarm call on Denison Street. The officers spotted a dark van without its lights on as it drove out of the parking lot and accelerated onto Esna Park Drive, according to a case summary released in December 2005 by the province's special investigations unit.
The SIU, a civilian agency, investigates cases of serious injuries and deaths involving police.
When the van reached Esna Park and Alden, it slammed into another van entering the intersection, the SIU said.
Three men got out of the van and ran from the collision scene. One man was arrested and an officer chased Mr. Black, who ran behind an industrial complex, the SIU said.
The officer found Mr. Black in a parking lot, told him he was under arrest and ordered him to show his hands, according to the SIU.

The officer had his gun drawn, but put it away when he discovered Mr. Black was cornered between storage trailers. When the officer moved in, Mr. Black struck and punched the officer in the chest, according to the SIU.
After he was hit several times, the officer realized Mr. Black was armed with a knife and had been stabbing the officer's bulletproof vest, the SIU said.
As the officer attempted to grasp Mr. Black's hand, he stabbed the officer on the top of his head, according to the SIU.
Mr. Black then pulled away and "dared the officer to shoot him", the SIU said. The officer pulled his gun and pepper-sprayed Mr. Black.
While the officer was dealing with Mr. Black, the York police helicopter flew over the scene and a call was put out for more police to respond to the area.

A second officer arrived to find Mr. Black moving toward the injured officer. The officer had his firearm drawn and pointed at Mr. Black. When the injured officer called out that Mr. Black was carrying a knife, Mr. Black lunged toward the second officer and "brought the knife down in a stabbing motion", according to the SIU.
The injured officer fired twice, striking Mr. Black in the abdomen.
Mr. Black died in hospital. The injured officer received medical treatment for a small cut on his head.
In the days following the shooting, Mr. Black's father said his son had made bad decisions as a teenager and ended up in jail as a juvenile.
He described his son as a "good, solid kid who loved his family."
The inquest is expected to hear from about a dozen witnesses, according to Dr. Bonita Porter, deputy chief coroner for inquests.
The inquest continues.
